{
  "analyses": [
    {
      "paper_id": "2005.13084",
      "title": "Learning with Weak Supervision for Email Intent Detection",
      "research_question": "Can noisy supervision derived from users' post-email interactions be combined with a small quantity of clean annotations to improve enterprise email intent detection?",
      "methodology": "The study uses the Avocado enterprise email corpus and formulates three binary intent-detection tasks: Request Information, Schedule Meeting, and Promise Action. Weak positive labels are generated from interaction heuristics such as replies with attachments, calendar interactions, and follow-up-related behavior, while a much smaller set of examples receives manual clean labels. The proposed Hydra architecture jointly learns from clean and weak supervision using separate prediction heads, label-noise correction, and self-paced learning, with experiments across multiple clean-to-weak data ratios and text encoders. The authors also test cross-domain transfer to Enron email.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "Behavioral weak-labeling functions are informative but substantially noisy: manual checks reported accuracies of about 0.675 for Request Information, 0.71 for Schedule Meeting, and 0.63 for Promise Action.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "2.3.2 Quality of Weak Labeling Functions"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Hydra consistently outperformed comparison methods that had access to both clean and weak examples, with the advantage especially useful when clean labels were scarce.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "4.2 Impact of Weak Supervision and 4.3 Impact of Clean Data Ratio"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Both self-paced learning and explicit weak-label correction contributed measurably: at a 10% clean ratio aggregate accuracy fell from 0.716 to 0.690 without self-paced learning and to 0.688 without label correction.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "4.4 Ablation Analysis"
        },
        {
          "finding": "For the Request Information task with a fixed clean set, increasing weakly labeled data improved reported accuracy from 0.688 with no weak examples to 0.804 when the full weak set was used.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "4.5 Additional Experiments"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Weak supervision learned from Avocado transferred to Enron; the reported zero-shot experiment using an Avocado-trained Hydra model achieved 0.738 accuracy on Enron.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "4.6 Domain Transfer"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Promise Action is treated as an email-level intent that the sender commits to a future action, but the experiments do not extract a structured action record containing an explicit owner span, deadline bound to that action, obligation polarity, or supporting evidence span.",
          "evidence_type": "unsupported",
          "section": "2.2 Dataset and 4 Experiments"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "The three weak-labeling heuristics have substantial false-positive and false-negative rates and depend on downstream user behavior rather than direct semantic annotation.",
        "Only three intent types are evaluated, so the experiments do not cover the broader range of workplace actions, decisions, delegations, or obligation states.",
        "The main task is intent classification rather than structured extraction of actor, action, deadline, condition, polarity, and evidence.",
        "The constructed datasets are balanced for evaluation and therefore do not directly represent natural intent base rates.",
        "Interaction signals are useful for training but generally become available only after a recipient has processed the email, so they are inappropriate as inference-time features.",
        "The domain-transfer evaluation is limited primarily to Avocado and Enron."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": true,

        "metrics_reported": true
      },

        "cross_domain_transfer_demonstrated": 0.97,
        "no_structured_owner_deadline_binding": 0.96
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "The paper studies Request Information, Schedule Meeting, and Promise Action intents in enterprise email.",
        "User interactions are converted into weak supervision rather than being used as inference-time features.",
        "Replying with an attachment is used as a weak indicator of a preceding information request.",
        "Calendar-related behavior is used to weakly supervise scheduling intent.",
        "Follow-up-related interaction is used as a proxy for Promise Action.",
        "Manual evaluation shows that all three weak-labeling functions contain considerable label noise.",
        "Hydra combines a small clean-labeled set with a substantially larger weak-labeled set.",
        "Self-paced learning controls which weak examples contribute during training.",
        "Increasing the amount of weak data improved performance in the Request Information experiment.",
        "Weak labels from Avocado could improve a model evaluated on Enron.",
        "The paper does not evaluate extraction of an owner-deadline-action tuple."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://arxiv.org/html/2005.13084",
      "access": "full_text"
    },
    {
      "paper_id": "doi-10-1145-3331184-3331260",
      "title": "Context-Aware Intent Identification in Email Conversations",
      "research_question": "Does incorporating the surrounding email-message context improve sentence-level identification of actionable workplace email intents?",
      "methodology": "The authors analyze the Avocado enterprise email corpus, initially annotating a random sample of 1,300 threads for multiple message-level intents and then constructing sentence-level datasets for Request Information, Schedule Meeting, and Promise Action. Human annotators identify whether an intent is present and highlight the text span where it is manifested; a separate experiment compares human judgments on 540 Request Information examples with and without access to the full email body. Models include sentence-only LR, SVM, and CNN baselines, simple sentence-plus-context models, and a Dynamic-Context Recurrent Neural Network using bidirectional GRUs and attention to model interactions between a target sentence and the rest of the message. Evaluation uses user-disjoint five-fold splits and F1.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "Enterprise messages frequently contain multiple intents: 55.2% of the analyzed messages had one intent, 35.8% had two, and 9.0% had three or more.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "3.1 Characterizing Types of Intents in Email"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Providing annotators with the full email body substantially improved Request Information recall, from 52.86 without context to 76.61 with context, while precision changed from 91.51 to 93.45.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "3.2 Effect of Contextual Information on Human Performance"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The context-sensitive DCRNN significantly outperformed the compared models on all three evaluated intents, reporting F1 values of 73.48 for Schedule Meeting, 80.42 for Promise Action, and 78.37 for Request Information.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.3 Results"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Simply concatenating conventional target-sentence and message-context features did not reliably help LR or SVM; the gains came from modeling interactions between the target sentence and relevant parts of context.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.3 Results"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Performance generally increased as more surrounding context was supplied, and the full email body produced the best DCRNN results among the tested context windows.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.3 Effect of the Context Size"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The annotation procedure explicitly highlighted the text span inside the email where an intent was manifested, providing direct evidence-span supervision even though the prediction task itself was sentence-level classification.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.1 Tasks"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The paper does not convert Promise Action or Request Action instances into structured records that separately resolve action owner, deadline-to-action attachment, conditions, or negated obligation state.",
          "evidence_type": "unsupported",
          "section": "3.1 Characterizing Types of Intents in Email and 5.1 Tasks"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "The experimental classification tasks cover only Request Information, Schedule Meeting, and Promise Action rather than the full intent taxonomy identified during corpus analysis.",
        "The intent taxonomy is explicitly non-comprehensive.",
        "The study is based on one enterprise corpus from a defunct IT company, and the authors note that workplace environment can affect intent distributions.",
        "The models identify intent-bearing sentences rather than extracting structured owner-action-deadline-condition relations.",
        "Although annotators highlight evidence spans, the reported models are evaluated as intent classifiers rather than exact span extractors.",
        "Simple temporal and user-history metadata explored by the authors did not materially improve the model, leaving richer metadata modeling for future work."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": false,
        "dataset_available": true,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "multiple_intents_are_common": 0.99,
        "context_improves_human_recall": 0.99,
        "dcrnn_outperforms_baselines": 0.99,
        "interaction_modeling_matters": 0.97,
        "full_message_context_best": 0.97,
        "evidence_spans_annotated": 0.99,
        "no_structured_owner_deadline_binding": 0.96
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "The study analyzes workplace email from the Avocado corpus.",
        "Email messages can contain multiple co-occurring intents.",
        "Request Action means that the sender asks a recipient to perform an activity.",
        "Promise Action means that the sender commits to performing an action.",
        "Annotators highlighted the text span where an intent appeared.",
        "Human annotators detected Request Information more completely when they could read the full email body.",
        "The DCRNN represents both a target sentence and the surrounding message context.",
        "Attention is used to determine which parts of context are relevant to tokens in the target sentence.",
        "The DCRNN outperformed sentence-only and simple context-concatenation baselines on the three main tasks.",
        "Larger context windows generally yielded better results.",
        "An ambiguous time expression can require surrounding context to distinguish a meeting time from a task deadline.",
        "The experiments do not explicitly bind a detected deadline to a structured action object."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/Wang_SIGIR19.pdf",
      "access": "full_text"

    {
      "paper_id": "doi-10-1145-3289600-3290984",
      "title": "Domain Adaptation for Commitment Detection in Email",
      "research_question": "How strongly does email-domain variation degrade sentence-level commitment detection, and can domain-adaptation methods learn commitment models that transfer more reliably between email corpora?",
      "methodology": "The study constructs sentence-level commitment datasets from Enron and Avocado emails, with crowdworkers labeling whether a highlighted sentence contains a specific action that the sender must or promises to complete; majority voting is used and reported inter-annotator agreement is Krippendorff's alpha of 0.73. The resulting datasets contain 65,398 Enron samples with 3,337 positives and 13,021 Avocado samples with 4,484 positives, with Avocado deliberately enriched for likely positive examples. Logistic-regression commitment classifiers using word or POS n-grams establish same-domain and cross-domain baselines, after which feature selection, linear feature mapping, importance sampling, and a neural autoencoder with task/domain-related objectives are evaluated for transfer. Precision, recall, F1, and AUC are reported with cross-validation.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "Commitments can be detected reasonably well when training and testing within the same corpus, with word-ngram LR F1 of 0.81 on Avocado and 0.78 on Enron.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "6.1 In-Domain Results"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Cross-domain transfer without adaptation degraded performance: Avocado-to-Enron F1 fell to 0.73 and Enron-to-Avocado F1 to 0.76, with particularly large AUC deterioration.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "6.2 Cross-Domain Results"
        },
        {
          "finding": "A classifier could distinguish Avocado from Enron sentences with F1 of 0.85, empirically demonstrating substantial corpus-specific lexical structure.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "6.3 Characterizing Inter-Domain Differences"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Sample-level importance weighting significantly improved transfer in both directions, and the tested feature-level adaptation methods also produced improvements in at least some transfer settings.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "6.3 Characterizing Inter-Domain Differences"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The proposed autoencoder benefited from its multiple loss components, and the variant using all available objectives achieved the strongest reported autoencoder performance.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "6.4 Transfer Learning Results"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The commitment label implicitly assigns responsibility to the email sender because a positive sentence is defined as an action the sender must or promises to complete, rather than performing open-ended owner extraction.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "3.1 Detecting Commitments in Email"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The study does not annotate or evaluate deadline-to-action links, conditional antecedents, obligation negation, or a separate evidence-span extraction task.",
          "evidence_type": "unsupported",
          "section": "3 Task and Data"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "The task is binary sentence classification rather than structured commitment extraction.",
        "Responsibility is effectively fixed to the sender by the annotation definition, so the work does not evaluate owner resolution for third parties, delegated owners, or multiple actors.",
        "Avocado was deliberately sampled using an existing classifier to increase positive examples, so its positive/negative distribution does not reflect the natural base rate.",
        "The Enron and Avocado commitment datasets have substantially different class distributions and sampling procedures, which complicates interpretation of transfer results.",
        "The authors report additional proprietary-corpus experiments but cannot provide the data or detailed results because of privacy and nondisclosure restrictions.",
        "Several adaptation approaches require labeled target-domain samples.",
        "The deep autoencoder is substantially more expensive to train than importance sampling.",
        "Deadline, condition, negation, and evidence-span relations are outside the evaluated label schema."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": false,
        "dataset_available": true,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "same_domain_commitment_detection_is_viable": 0.99,
        "domain_shift_hurts": 0.99,
        "domains_are_lexically_distinguishable": 0.99,
        "adaptation_improves_transfer": 0.98,
        "autoencoder_losses_help": 0.96,
        "owner_is_implicitly_sender": 0.99,
        "no_deadline_condition_polarity_schema": 0.98
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "A commitment is modeled as a sentence containing a specific action the sender must or promises to perform.",
        "Crowdworkers provide binary commitment labels at sentence level.",
        "The annotation protocol uses majority agreement among annotators.",
        "Enron contains many more annotated samples but a much lower positive rate than Avocado.",
        "Avocado was enriched with candidate positives using a previously trained classifier.",
        "Within-domain commitment classification performs substantially better than unadapted cross-domain use.",
        "A domain classifier can accurately distinguish Enron from Avocado sentences.",
        "Importance sampling improves commitment transfer in both tested directions.",
        "The proposed autoencoder aims to learn a more domain-independent sentence representation.",
        "Most transfer configurations requiring neural adaptation use some target-domain supervision.",
        "The paper does not extract deadlines or conditions associated with commitments."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/AzarbonyadWSDM2019.pdf",
      "access": "full_text"
    },
    {
      "paper_id": "doi-10-1109-scc-2013-62",
      "title": "Monitoring Commitments in People-Driven Service Engagements",
      "research_question": "Can commitments and their lifecycle operations be automatically identified and tracked from real-world email and chat conversations in people-driven service engagements?",
      "methodology": "The paper defines commitments as structured debtor-creditor relationships with antecedent and consequent components and models lifecycle operations including creation, detachment, discharge, cancellation, and delegation or subcontracting. Its extraction pipeline parses sentences, identifies tasks and participants, applies linguistic and dependency-based heuristics, and then uses Naive Bayes, logistic regression, or SVM classifiers to identify commitment operations. Evaluation uses 4,161 Enron email sentences and 7,154 sentences from 271 HP IT-support chat conversations, manually labeled by two annotators, with ten-fold cross-validation followed by evaluation on disjoint test sets. A prototype integrates parsing, feature extraction, prediction, and user confirmation.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "The representation explicitly separates a commitment's debtor, creditor, antecedent, and consequent, making this paper directly relevant to structured responsibility assignment rather than only action-intent classification.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "II Commitments and IV Understanding Commitments"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Although the formal model supports conditional commitments, the operational extraction treatment states that most examined email and chat interactions are taken to indicate unconditional commitments, so empirical conditional-antecedent extraction is limited.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "IV.B Commitment Creation"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The approach derives owner-like roles explicitly: task performer maps to commitment debtor and beneficiary maps to creditor, while conversation roles and parsed linguistic structure help identify those parameters.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "IV Task and Commitment Creation and V Approach"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Deadline expressions are included as a feature indicating commitment creation or delegation, but the evaluated representation does not separately extract and score an explicit deadline span bound to a particular consequent.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "V Approach to Identify and Monitor Commitments"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Negation is operationalized primarily as evidence of cancellation: an existing commitment whose matching action appears with a negative dependency such as 'not' can be classified as canceled.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "V.H Identifying Cancellations"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Creation detection is much stronger than rare lifecycle-operation detection on independent data: email F1 was 0.90 for commissive creation and 0.86 for directive creation, while email discharge and cancellation obtained zero F1; chat discharge reached 0.69 while cancellation remained zero.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "VI.C Results"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Annotations and predictions are primarily sentence-level operation labels rather than explicit evidence-span boundaries for each extracted debtor, creditor, action, deadline, or negation cue.",
          "evidence_type": "unsupported",
          "section": "VI.B Labeling Data"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "Lifecycle-operation classes are highly imbalanced; cancellation and delegation examples are extremely sparse.",
        "Independent-test performance is strong for creation but weak or zero for several lifecycle operations.",
        "The formal model allows conditional commitments, but the implemented extraction largely concentrates on unconditional cases.",
        "Deadline presence is used as a feature rather than evaluated as an explicit deadline-to-action relation.",
        "Negation is mainly interpreted as cancellation of a previously created commitment and does not constitute a general treatment of negated obligations or prohibitions.",
        "Correct discharge, cancellation, and subcontract detection depends on finding and matching a previous commitment across conversational context.",
        "The email evaluation is drawn from conversations involving one Enron employee and a limited set of correspondents.",
        "The HP IT-support chat corpus and the paper's manual annotations are not documented as publicly released.",
        "The annotation scheme does not provide independently evaluated evidence-span extraction."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": false,
        "dataset_available": false,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "structured_debtor_creditor_representation": 0.99,
        "conditional_model_but_unconditional_empirics": 0.97,
        "explicit_owner_assignment": 0.99,
        "deadline_used_only_as_feature": 0.95,
        "negation_used_for_cancellation": 0.99,
        "creation_far_easier_than_rare_lifecycle_ops": 0.99,
        "no_span_level_evaluation": 0.96
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "A commitment relates a debtor to a creditor for a consequent under an antecedent.",
        "Commitments can be created, discharged, canceled, and delegated or subcontracted.",
        "The task performer is used as the commitment debtor and the beneficiary as the creditor.",
        "The approach parses email and chat sentences before extracting task and commitment features.",
        "Modal verbs and action verbs are used as commitment-creation signals.",
        "Deadline expressions are treated as features associated with creation or delegation.",
        "Past-tense actions can signal discharge when they match an existing commitment.",
        "Negative dependencies can signal cancellation of an existing commitment.",
        "Two annotators labeled email and chat sentences for commitment operations.",
        "Creation classes are much more frequent than cancellation and delegation classes.",
        "Independent-test results show substantially better creation detection than cancellation or discharge detection.",
        "The prototype is designed to display inferred commitments for user verification."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://www.csc2.ncsu.edu/faculty/mpsingh/papers/societal/SCC-13-people.pdf",
      "access": "full_text"
    },
    {
      "paper_id": "1909.10094",
      "title": "Deep Structured Neural Network for Event Temporal Relation Extraction",
      "research_question": "Can a jointly trained neural and structured-prediction model improve event-event temporal relation extraction by combining contextual representations with global consistency constraints?",
      "methodology": "The model combines a neural pairwise scoring network with a structured SVM that performs joint prediction subject to temporal constraints. Token representations use pretrained BERT and POS embeddings followed by a bidirectional LSTM, while structured inference incorporates symmetry and transitivity and, for TCR, temporal-causal constraints through integer linear programming. Experiments are conducted on TB-Dense, MATRES, and TCR, with augmented reverse-order training pairs, multiple random seeds, micro-averaged and temporal-awareness metrics, ablations, and qualitative error analysis. This is not a workplace email/chat study; its relevance to the review topic is methodological, especially for temporal relation binding and treatment of negation.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "The global structured model improved over its local neural counterpart across all three temporal-relation datasets, and the TCR improvement of more than 1.2 F1 points was reported as statistically significant.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5 Results and Analysis"
        },
        {
          "finding": "With BERT representations, reported global-model F1 values were 63.2 on TB-Dense, 81.7 on MATRES, and 80.9 on TCR, exceeding the cited previous state of the art.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "6.3 Effect of BERT Representations"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Ablations show that transitivity constraints consistently improve results, while symmetry-related augmentation and constraints improve robustness when relation direction is reversed.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "6.1 Effect of the Structured Constraints"
        },
        {
          "finding": "BERT representations account for a substantial part of the gain, although the structured architecture using GloVe remained competitive or superior to previous systems on several datasets.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "6.3 Effect of BERT Representations"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Negation remained a significant failure mode: 20% of a manually analyzed sample of common errors was categorized as negation-related, and the authors explicitly identify better handling of negation and hypothetical language as future work.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.4 Error Analysis and 7 Conclusion"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The annotated units are event pairs and their temporal relations, which provides relational supervision useful for temporal binding but does not directly identify workplace actions, owners, obligations, or deadline expressions.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "4 Experimental Setup"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The experiments do not demonstrate deadline-to-action extraction in workplace communication or conditional/negated obligation extraction; applying this architecture to such relations would require a different annotation schema and domain evaluation.",
          "evidence_type": "unsupported",
          "section": "4 Experimental Setup and 5 Results and Analysis"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "The datasets are temporal-relation benchmarks rather than workplace email or chat corpora.",
        "The task predicts relations between pre-identified events rather than jointly extracting actions, deadlines, owners, and obligation states.",
        "The architecture considers event pairs within the same or neighboring sentences under the experimental setup.",
        "Densely annotated temporal datasets are relatively small.",
        "Error analysis shows unresolved dependence on broader world knowledge.",
        "Negation and intention or hypothetical expressions remain prominent error sources.",
        "Event-event temporal relations are not equivalent to explicit deadline-to-action binding.",
        "The paper does not evaluate ownership, delegation, deontic polarity, or workplace evidence-span annotation."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": false,
        "dataset_available": true,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "structured_global_prediction_improves_results": 0.99,
        "strong_benchmark_performance": 0.99,
        "transitivity_and_symmetry_help": 0.98,
        "bert_contributes_large_gain": 0.99,
        "negation_is_failure_mode": 0.99,
        "event_pair_supervision_not_action_schema": 0.99,
        "workplace_deadline_binding_not_evaluated": 0.99
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "The model combines neural pairwise scoring with structured global inference.",
        "BERT representations and a bidirectional LSTM provide contextual features for event pairs.",
        "The structured layer imposes temporal consistency constraints.",
        "Symmetry and transitivity are explicitly represented in structured inference.",
        "Experiments use the TB-Dense, MATRES, and TCR temporal-relation datasets.",
        "The global model improves over the local model across the three datasets.",
        "Transitivity constraints consistently improve performance in the reported ablations.",
        "BERT provides a large performance gain over GloVe representations.",
        "Some errors require broader contextual or commonsense knowledge.",
        "Negation can reverse or otherwise alter the inferred temporal relation.",
        "Intention events are another identified source of temporal-relation errors.",
        "The paper does not study email action ownership or deontic obligation extraction."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://arxiv.org/html/1909.10094",
      "access": "full_text"
    }
  ],
  "skipped": []
}
